analysis.one_liner: Taxes hedge fund and private equity managers' carried-interest pay at ordinary income rates.
analysis.headline: The Carried Interest Fairness Act was introduced in February 2025 and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee with no hearings, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Hedge fund and private equity partners are typically paid with a share of their fund's profits, called carried interest. Under current law the tax code treats that pay as a capital gain, which is taxed at a lower rate than regular work income. The bill would reclassify carried interest as ordinary income — the same treatment as a salary — and also subject it to self-employment taxes. It would raise revenue from a small group of very high earners, and the money would otherwise be available to the Treasury for whatever Congress chooses to fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit broadly but diffusely: income from fund managers' work would be taxed like everyone else's work income, adding revenue that could reduce deficits or fund public programs. Federal, state, and local governments that lose revenue to the current treatment also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill recharacterizes net capital gain from carried interest in investment partnerships as ordinary income, so it is taxed at the same rates as wages rather than the lower capital gains rates [S2].
It extends the 'hot asset rule' so that money or property received for selling a carried interest is treated as ordinary income rather than capital gain [S2].
It applies self-employment taxes to carried interest income, closing a gap where this work income avoids payroll taxes that ordinary workers pay [S2].

It closes several workarounds, including treating distributions in exchange for other partnership property as taxable sales and imposing a doubled 40 percent penalty on underpayments tied to avoidance schemes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: General partners at private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate investment firms, whose share of fund profits would be taxed at top ordinary income rates and be subject to self-employment tax. These are among the highest earners in the country.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund partners

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts gains allocated to a domestic C corporation from the new rules [S3], which tax lawyers would likely treat as a roadmap to restructure partnerships and shift carry into corporate form, complicating enforcement.

The provision denying carried-interest income 'qualifying income' status for publicly traded partnerships includes a transition that does not begin until 10 years after enactment [S3], so some structures would keep the current treatment for a decade.

The rules are highly technical, with extensive elections, safe harbors, and Secretary-of-the-Treasury discretion [S3], which supporters of the current treatment argue invites disputes and litigation even if the policy goal is sound.

Fund managers would argue the current lower rate reflects the risk of their capital-like stake; the bill's own machinery — defining 'qualified capital interests' that keep capital-gains treatment — is an acknowledgment that distinguishing true invested capital from labor income is difficult to draw cleanly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — taxing a manager's share of profits from managing other people's money at the same rate as work income — is a defensible fairness fix that raises revenue from a narrow, high-income group. The costs are concentrated on those managers and largely involve complexity and avoidance risk rather than public harm. The main weakness is design: the corporation carve-out and the 10-year transition would blunt the bill and push income into new structures.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2025 and has sat there with no hearings, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2025 on February 6, 2025, for herself and Representative Don Beyer [S1].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S5].
Only two House Democrats cosponsored the bill alongside the sponsor [S4], so it has minimal support even within its own party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity and hedge fund partners are better off so far: the current treatment of carried interest as lower-taxed capital gain remains untouched because the bill has not moved in committee. Ordinary taxpayers are no worse off than before, but have gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax carried interest as ordinary income on February 6, 2025.

for.name: Rep. Don Beyer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the only original cosponsor named at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled in the year since the bill arrived.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; with a 223-seat Republican majority, no tax increase on investment managers would reach a vote without leadership's say-so.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship and cosponsorship are entirely Democratic — a Democrat introduced the bill and both cosponsors are Democrats — and no Republican has signed on, while Republicans hold a 223-seat House majority and control the Ways and Means agenda.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their signature pay — a share of fund profits taxed as capital gain — would be taxed as ordinary income and become subject to self-employment tax. Managers oppose this because it raises their tax bill on labor-like income by a large margin; for the public, it is additional revenue.
The bill's definition of specified assets includes real estate held for rental or investment, so real estate sponsors using carried interest would face the same higher tax treatment.
The bill explicitly sweeps SPACs into the investment-management rules and would tax sponsor promotional interests as ordinary income.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action more than a year after referral, only two cosponsors, and a Ways and Means majority whose tax priorities run the other way, the bill is very likely to die quietly at the end of this Congress without a vote, as every carried-interest repeal bill of the last decade has.
